transcript.text: Our Dyson (one of the V ones, purple bits) keeps cutting out after about 5-10 seconds. Not every time - some days it does a whole room fine. It's maybe 5 years old. Already cleaned the filter and checked for blockages. Battery or something else?

At ~5 years, the battery is a strong possibility, but the pattern matters:

• Stops abruptly after 5–10 seconds, then will run again after releasing/re-pulling trigger: often battery, battery connection, or trigger/switch.
• “Pulses” on/off repeatedly while the trigger is held: more often an airflow restriction — including one in the wand, cleaner head, cyclone/bin inlet, or a filter that is still damp.
• Only happens with the floor head fitted: likely the motorised head, its brush bar, or the wand/head electrical contacts.
• Mostly happens on Max/Boost mode: battery is especially likely; an ageing battery may still manage normal mode some days but collapse under higher load.

A few useful tests, in order:

1. Fully charge it, then try it with no wand or floor head attached — just the main handheld unit.
• If it cuts out: battery / machine / trigger issue.
• If it runs normally: inspect the wand and floor head more closely.

2. Try it with the wand but no head, then with the head attached.
   Check right through the wand (a torch helps), around the inlet behind the bin, and under/around the roller. Fine fluff can form a plug that is not obvious.

3. Remove and refit the battery and attachments if your version allows it. Wipe the electrical contacts gently with a dry cloth. Look for loose fit, corrosion, or damaged pins.

4. Make sure the filter has dried completely. After washing it should air-dry for at least 24 hours — longer in a cool house. A slightly damp filter can cause poor airflow/cut-outs.

5. Check whether it is hot when it stops. If the body/motor area is getting unusually warm, leave it to cool and re-check for an airflow blockage.

If it cuts out even as a bare handheld after a full charge, especially if it is worse in Max mode, I’d put the battery at the top of the list. Five years is a very normal age for a Dyson cordless battery to start losing capacity or voltage stability. A replacement battery is usually much cheaper than replacing the vacuum — ideally use a genuine Dyson part or a reputable supplier compatible with the exact model.

Find the model on the silver/white rating label, usually behind the bin or under the battery (e.g. V7, V8, V10). That matters because “purple bits” appears on several Dyson V models and their batteries are not interchangeable.

One safety note: if the battery case is swollen, cracked, unusually hot, smells odd, or the vacuum behaves erratically while charging, stop using/charging it and replace the battery rather than trying to troubleshoot further.

Label says SV11. Without the wand or head it still cuts out sometimes, just less often. It's a clean stop, not pulsing, and the filter dried for 48 hours. Battery isn't swollen or hot. Is it worth spending £60+ on a new battery?

SV11 is a Dyson V7. Given:

• it is around 5 years old,
• it cuts out cleanly rather than pulsing,
• it does it even with no wand/head fitted,
• but it is less likely to do so with less load,

…the battery is the most likely cause. An ageing lithium battery can look completely normal — no swelling, heat or obvious damage — but its voltage drops sharply when the motor demands power, and the battery protection circuit shuts it off. The extra load of the wand/head makes that more likely.

A blockage usually causes the characteristic rapid pulsing/surging, rather than a clean stop.

Before spending £60+, I’d do these final checks:

1. Fully charge it, then use it as a bare handheld on normal power.
   If it stops in seconds/minutes but will run again after a brief pause, that strongly points to battery voltage sag.

2. Note the lights when it cuts out.
• Flashing blue / battery indicator behaviour around the cut-out supports battery.
• A persistent flashing red light can indicate a battery fault.
• No unusual lights does not rule out the battery — many weak V7 batteries simply shut down.

3. Clean/reseat the battery contacts.
   Remove the battery if yours has the three screw fitting, wipe contacts with a dry lint-free cloth, and make sure it is firmly screwed back on. Also inspect the charger cable/socket for looseness.

4. Try normal vs Max mode.
   If Max makes it fail virtually immediately while normal mode sometimes works, that is very persuasive battery evidence.

Is it worth replacing? Probably, yes — if the rest of the V7 is in good shape. A V7 with a new battery can still be perfectly useful for several more years, and a battery is usually the economical repair versus replacing the whole vacuum. On your symptoms I’d say it is a reasonable bet, rather than blindly replacing parts.

I would buy either:

• a genuine Dyson battery, if the price difference is acceptable; or
• a reputable UK replacement with a proper warranty and easy returns.

Avoid the very cheapest unbranded marketplace batteries: capacity claims are often optimistic and lithium-pack quality matters. A replacement sold with a 12-month warranty is useful here — if the fault remains unchanged, you can return it and look next at the trigger/switch or main body electronics.

The main alternative is the trigger/switch assembly, which can become intermittent on V7s. That is more likely if stopping relates to how you hold or squeeze the trigger, rather than whether the machine is under load. But your “less often without wand/head” observation makes the battery the better first bet.
